story.title: The preparation matters as much as the rinse.
story.text: A site visit should identify coatings, loose material, nearby planting, runoff, and access. “More pressure” is not a universal answer.

guide.title: Know the surface. Respect the setting.
guide.intro: A well-scoped project avoids surprises for both the property owner and the crew.

notes.title: Identify the material
notes.text: Concrete, brick, siding, timber, and painted finishes do not respond the same way. Share any sealers, coatings, damage, or manufacturer care instructions.

notes.title: Set realistic expectations
notes.text: Some staining, oxidation, or weathering may remain. A real provider should discuss likely results and consider a test area where appropriate.

notes.title: Plan access and drainage
notes.text: Identify water access, electrical fixtures, nearby plants, and how runoff will be handled. Local requirements belong in the site-specific plan.

notes.title: Get the space ready
notes.text: Move loose items and vehicles, close openings, and flag fragile areas. Ask what the crew will handle and what needs to be ready before arrival.

faq.a: Not necessarily. Results depend on material, age, previous treatments, and the stain. This example makes no guaranteed restoration claims.

faq.q: Can you clean painted or delicate surfaces?
faq.a: They require a material-specific assessment. A real provider should confirm a suitable method or recommend a specialist when needed.
